final_proof:
Let the observations be \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_n\), and write
\[
 \bar a=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n a_k,
 \qquad
 \bar b=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n b_k.
\]
Because \(\mathbf C\) is assumed to be the correlation matrix of these two sequences, the relevant correlations are defined; in particular, neither sequence has zero centered sum of squares. Put
\[
 S_a=\sum_{k=1}^n(a_k-\bar a)^2>0,
 \qquad
 S_b=\sum_{k=1}^n(b_k-\bar b)^2>0.
\]
By the definition of the Pearson correlation matrix,
\[
 \mathbf C=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n(a_k-\bar a)(a_k-\bar a)}{\sqrt{S_aS_a}}
 &
 \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n(a_k-\bar a)(b_k-\bar b)}{\sqrt{S_aS_b}}
 \\
 \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n(b_k-\bar b)(a_k-\bar a)}{\sqrt{S_bS_a}}
 &
 \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n(b_k-\bar b)(b_k-\bar b)}{\sqrt{S_bS_b}}
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The two off-diagonal numerators are equal because multiplication of real numbers is commutative, and their denominators are equal because \(\sqrt{S_aS_b}=\sqrt{S_bS_a}\). Hence \(C_{12}=C_{21}\). (The equality of the diagonal entries with their own transposes is automatic.) Therefore \(C_{ij}=C_{ji}\) for every \(i,j\in\{1,2\}\), so \(\mathbf C\) is symmetric.

Finally,
\[
 C_{11}=\frac{S_a}{\sqrt{S_a^2}}=\frac{S_a}{S_a}=1,
 \qquad
 C_{22}=\frac{S_b}{\sqrt{S_b^2}}=\frac{S_b}{S_b}=1,
\]
where positivity of \(S_a,S_b\) was used in \(\sqrt{S_a^2}=S_a\) and \(\sqrt{S_b^2}=S_b\). Thus every entry on the main diagonal of \(\mathbf C\) is \(1\), as claimed.
